claims.text: The alloy is initially a single-phase high-entropy alloy.
Brittle behavior in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy is governed by the formation of deleterious phases.
Laves phases and other intermetallic compounds are deleterious phases that can cause brittle behavior.
Changes in alloy composition can alter phase stability and promote phase decomposition or additional phases in high-entropy alloys.
Processing temperature can cause an initially solid-solution high-entropy alloy to decompose and form Laves phases.
Changes in service environment can cause deleterious intermetallic phases to form.
The proposed mechanism applies under high-temperature service conditions.
The proposed mechanism applies under high-stress service conditions.
The proposed mechanism applies in corrosive service environments.
Laves phases or other intermetallic compounds constitute the structural mediator of embrittlement.
Nucleation and growth of deleterious phases reduce toughness and cause embrittlement.
The predicted brittle behavior will be manifested as reduced toughness.
The predicted brittle behavior will increase susceptibility to cracking or fracture.
The initial single-phase alloy has a favorable strength–ductility combination.
There are tolerable limits of composition, processing, and environment below which deleterious phases do not form.
The exact mechanisms and kinetics of deleterious-phase formation and their effects on mechanical properties are not fully understood.
A controlled comparison varying composition, processing conditions, and service environment can test the hypothesis using microstructural, mechanical, and corrosion measurements.
Failure to observe deleterious phases together with retention of the initial strength–ductility combination would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis makes deleterious-phase formation the cause of brittle behavior, so observing neither such phases nor property degradation is consistent with the hypothesis rather than a falsification. A decisive falsification would instead require phase formation without the predicted toughness loss, or toughness loss in a phase-free matched specimen.
